::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Benchmarking the Double-Entry Intraclass Correlation as an Index of the Similarity between Correlation Profiles

text.text: Copilot and ChatGPT 5.6 have been used to create the R code for the simulation studies.
I have reviewed, edited, and validated the accuracy of the output and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.
The Nomological Network
The nomological network of a measurement instrument describes the pattern of relationships between scores of this instrument and scores of other measurement tools.
It can be formalized as a vector of bivariate correlations between the test score for the construct under scrutiny and scores of external variables.

The variables shaping the empirical nomological network, in turn, can be measured with diverse data sources, such as selfreported, behavioral, physiological, or other-reported information (Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Cronbach & Meehl, 1955).
text.formatted: The variables shaping the empirical nomological network, in turn, can be measured with diverse data sources, such as selfreported, behavioral, physiological, or other-reported information <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cronbach & Meehl, 1955)</ref>.

text.text: Constructing a nomological network for a newly devised or reevaluated measure has been the standard procedure for the investigation of evidence in favor of or against construct validity because the nomological network reflects an indicator of what the measurement instrument under scrutiny actually assesses.

If the test score of the measurement instrument manifests a set of theoretically expected associations with the external variables within the nomological network, it is usually inferred that the target measure assesses what it purports to (American Educational Research Association et al., 2014; Cronbach & Meehl, 1955).
text.formatted: If the test score of the measurement instrument manifests a set of theoretically expected associations with the external variables within the nomological network, it is usually inferred that the target measure assesses what it purports to <ref type="bibr">(American Educational Research Association et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cronbach & Meehl, 1955)</ref>.

text.text: Mere investigations of isolated bivariate relations with external variables, however, are associated with the risk to establish a landscape of redundant or insufficiently validated measures when researchers frequently pay little attention to overlaps with already existing constructs and measures (Hanfstingl et al., 2025; Lawson & Robins, 2021).
text.formatted: Mere investigations of isolated bivariate relations with external variables, however, are associated with the risk to establish a landscape of redundant or insufficiently validated measures when researchers frequently pay little attention to overlaps with already existing constructs and measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hanfstingl et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lawson & Robins, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, ostensibly alternative measures for a construct under scrutiny often fail to tap into the same concept, or measures purported to tap into a new construct in fact repackage existing concepts.

Considering whether psychometrical scales actually assess what they purport to, systematic investigations of such jingle fallacies (i.e., measures/constructs intended to tap into the same concept in fact measure different constructs [Thorndike, 1904]) and jangle fallacies (i.e., measures/constructs with different measurement intentions in fact assess the same concepts [Kelley, 1927]) have commenced only recently (Hanfstingl et al., 2025).

text.text: In these analyses, comparisons between empirical sets of correlations (hereafter correlation profiles) take a central role beyond the analyses of mere intercorrelations.
That is, high (low) correlations between potentially jingled/jangled scores do not necessarily cause identical (different) correlation profiles involving external variables (Lawson & Robins, 2021).
text.formatted: That is, high (low) correlations between potentially jingled/jangled scores do not necessarily cause identical (different) correlation profiles involving external variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lawson & Robins, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, the degree to which two scores are correlated only determines the range of differences between the correlations of these scores with other variables (Yule, 1922).
text.formatted: Instead, the degree to which two scores are correlated only determines the range of differences between the correlations of these scores with other variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Yule, 1922)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, Gonzalez et al. (2021) demonstrated that, given an almost perfect correlation (r12 = .998) between two variables (say, two extraversion scales) and a correlation between the first variable with an external variable (say, frequency of experiencing positive mood) of rY, X1 = .30, the second variable can yield correlations with the external variable within a range between .24 and .36.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gonzalez et al. (2021)</ref> demonstrated that, given an almost perfect correlation (r12 = .998) between two variables (say, two extraversion scales) and a correlation between the first variable with an external variable (say, frequency of experiencing positive mood) of rY, X1 = .30, the second variable can yield correlations with the external variable within a range between .24 and .36.

text.text: If, however, the two variables (again, two extraversion scales) were correlated at a more realistic yet still high level, such as r12 = .70, and the first was correlated with the external variable at rY, X1 = .30, possible correlations between the second variable and the external variable would range from -.47 to .89.

Finding a set of similar relations of the two variables with a reasonable set of external variables, despite the hypothetical range of possible correlations, would pose an indicator of redundancy (Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Gonzalez et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Finding a set of similar relations of the two variables with a reasonable set of external variables, despite the hypothetical range of possible correlations, would pose an indicator of redundancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cronbach & Meehl, 1955;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gonzalez et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Instead of inspecting the mere correlation between two measures, it is recommended to compare the profiles of correlations with external variables.

Therein, the coefficients within the correlation profiles of measures for the same construct should be similar, whereas the coefficients in the correlation profiles of measures for disparate constructs should not (Blötner, 2025; Lawson & Robins, 2021; Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019).
text.formatted: Therein, the coefficients within the correlation profiles of measures for the same construct should be similar, whereas the coefficients in the correlation profiles of measures for disparate constructs should not <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blötner, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lawson & Robins, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To address the question of whether two or more correlation profiles are (almost) identical, existing methodological guidelines recommend correlation difference tests for dependent correlations (Blötner, 2025; Gonzalez et al., 2021; Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019).
text.formatted: To address the question of whether two or more correlation profiles are (almost) identical, existing methodological guidelines recommend correlation difference tests for dependent correlations <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blötner, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gonzalez et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: According to the concomitant logic, two scores reflect the same construct if they exhibit, by and large, equivalent correlations with a reasonable set of external variables.
This approach is related to several problems, however, that limit its utility to gauge the equivalence vis-à-vis distinctiveness of correlation profiles.

First, the statistical power to detect an existing correlation difference depends on a plethora of aspects, such as the sample size, the minimum difference between the correlations above which one assumes a substantial difference, the intercorrelation of the compared scores, and the desired α-level (see Blötner, 2025, for a pertinent recommendation for power analyses in the context of examinations of assumed jingle and jangle fallacies).

text.text: In this regard, Blötner (2025) illustrated that methodologically sound examinations of jingle and jangle fallacies require sample sizes that are frequently not achieved in published research.
text.formatted: In this regard, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Blötner (2025)</ref> illustrated that methodologically sound examinations of jingle and jangle fallacies require sample sizes that are frequently not achieved in published research.

text.text: Second, but relatedly, it is barely possible to propose a rule of thumb for a critical ratio of significant versus non-significant correlation differences above which construct redundancy is assumed to hold and below which construct uniqueness is assumed.
More specifically, it stands to reason that it is hardly possible to compare two conceptually unrelated endeavors to examine particular jangle fallacies (Blötner, 2025).
text.formatted: More specifically, it stands to reason that it is hardly possible to compare two conceptually unrelated endeavors to examine particular jangle fallacies <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blötner, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Alternative guidelines (e.g., Blötner, 2025; Lawson & Robins, 2021; Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019), thus, recommend combined approaches that supplement examinations of correlation differences with a descriptive overall index of the similarity between two correlation profiles.
text.formatted: Alternative guidelines (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Blötner, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lawson & Robins, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019)</ref>, thus, recommend combined approaches that supplement examinations of correlation differences with a descriptive overall index of the similarity between two correlation profiles.

text.text: Generally speaking, any kind of profile can be described through three parameterselevation, scatter, and shape (Cronbach & Gleser, 1953).
text.formatted: Generally speaking, any kind of profile can be described through three parameterselevation, scatter, and shape <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cronbach & Gleser, 1953)</ref>.

text.text: Elevation and scatter denote the central tendency and the dispersion of the coefficients within a profile, respectively, such as the mean and the variance across the elements.
Shape reflects the pattern of peaks and valleys of the trajectory of the elements of a profile across the utilized correlates, but it is usually not quantified through a comprehensive index.
An index that quantifies the similarity between correlation profiles should acknowledge the three aforementioned characteristics.

At first glance, the most straightforward way to quantify the similarity between two vectors of correlation coefficients with a single index would be computing the bivariate correlation between them (e.g., Pearson's product-moment correlation r or Spearman's rank correlation ρ).
These indices, however, quantify the (dis)similarity of the rank order, not the elementwise correspondence between the elements of the vectors themselves.
For instance, consider the correlation profiles X = [.05, .19, .57, .34] and X' = [.35, .49, .87, .64].
Each element of X' reflects an element from X to which a constant of .30 was added.

Since the rank order remains identical if a constant is added, bivariate correlations between X and X' would indicate perfect similarity (e.g., r = 1.00)-despite an obvious lack of element-wise correspondence.

Accordingly, bivariate correlation coefficients are maximally sensitive to shape (dis)similarity but insensitive to scatter and/or elevation (dis)similarity (Furr, 2010), rendering them unsuitable to acknowledge shape, scatter, and elevation simultaneously.
text.formatted: Accordingly, bivariate correlation coefficients are maximally sensitive to shape (dis)similarity but insensitive to scatter and/or elevation (dis)similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Furr, 2010)</ref>, rendering them unsuitable to acknowledge shape, scatter, and elevation simultaneously.

text.text: Consistent with earlier research on the agreement between the correlation profiles of different measures (e.g., Blötner, 2025; Gonzalez et al., 2021; Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019), the similarity between correlation profiles (or profile similarity) is herein understood as the overall degree of element-wise correspondence between correlation profiles.
text.formatted: Consistent with earlier research on the agreement between the correlation profiles of different measures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Blötner, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gonzalez et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019)</ref>, the similarity between correlation profiles (or profile similarity) is herein understood as the overall degree of element-wise correspondence between correlation profiles.

text.text: In turn, correlation profiles are deemed different if-by and large-considerable element-wise discrepancies occur.

Accordingly, to justify conclusions about the redundancy of correlation profiles due to their overall similarity (Blötner, 2025; Gonzalez et al., 2021; Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019), (almost equal) magnitudes of elevation and scatter as well as (almost equal) visual shapes are required (Cronbach & Gleser, 1953).
text.formatted: Accordingly, to justify conclusions about the redundancy of correlation profiles due to their overall similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blötner, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gonzalez et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019)</ref>, (almost equal) magnitudes of elevation and scatter as well as (almost equal) visual shapes are required <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cronbach & Gleser, 1953)</ref>.

text.text: Figure 1 illustrates two pairs of profiles.

text.text: The profiles illustrated in panel A do not comply with the aforementioned criteria of similarity because the two profiles agree in shape and scatter, but they differ in their levels of elevations (induced by adding .30 to each element of the solid-lined profile).

The difference in terms of the levels of elevation indicates that the respective scores for which the correlations with other variables are illustrated with dashed and solid lines are differently related to the ten criteria, suggesting that the scores pertain to different constructs (Blötner, 2025; Gonzalez et al., 2021; Lawson & Robins, 2021).

text.text: Panel B, in turn, entails only negligible differences between the trajectories regarding shape, scatter, and elevation.

Therefore, the corresponding profiles are deemed highly similar (if not virtually identical), and researchers would conclude that the underlying measures tap into the same construct (Blötner, 2025; Gonzalez et al., 2021; Lawson & Robins, 2021).

text.text: Note.
In panel A, the profile depicted with a dashed line reflects an upward shift of the profile depicted with a solid line by adding .30 to each element.
In panel B, the profile depicted with a dashed line was constructed by adding random numbers from a range between -.03 and .03 to the respective elements of the profile depicted with a solid line.
An index recommended in the aforementioned guidelines is the Double-Entry Intraclass Correlation (ICCDE; McCrae, 2008).
text.formatted: An index recommended in the aforementioned guidelines is the Double-Entry Intraclass Correlation (ICCDE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">McCrae, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: For its computation, the vector of the k elements of the first profile (e.g., A = [a1, a2, a3, …, ak]) is appended to the vector of the k elements of the second profile (B = [b1, b2, b3, …, bk]) and vice versa.

text.text: The ICCDE reflects the bivariate correlation between the double-entered vectors AB = [a1, a2, a3, …, ak, b1, b2, b3, …, bk] and BA = [b1, b2, b3, …, bk, a1, a2, a3, …, ak], rAB, BA (McCrae, 2008).
text.formatted: The ICCDE reflects the bivariate correlation between the double-entered vectors AB = [a1, a2, a3, …, ak, b1, b2, b3, …, bk] and BA = [b1, b2, b3, …, bk, a1, a2, a3, …, ak], rAB, BA <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(McCrae, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: An ICCDE of +1 is usually interpreted as perfect agreement, an ICCDE of -1 as perfect inverse agreement, and an ICCDE of 0 as absence of systematic correspondence.
Whether inverse agreement should be viewed as a form of similarity or dissimilarity depends on the substantive research question.

Earlier studies recommended general cutoffs, such as |ICCDE| ≥ .60 (Lawson & Robins, 2021) or .80 (Thielmann & Hilbig, 2019), whereas many published studies applied a cutoff as high as |ICCDE| > .90 as an indicator of construct redundancy (e.g., Baerg MacDonald & Schermer, 2025; Blötner & Mokros, 2023; Hart et al., 2023; Hyatt et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2017; Mund et al., 2023; Samuel et al., 2012; Somma et al., 2021; Vize et al., 2021; see Blötner, 2025, for an overview).

text.text: Because the ICCDE is mathematically related to the correlation between profiles, its is often heavily influenced by shape similarity (Furr, 2010).
text.formatted: Because the ICCDE is mathematically related to the correlation between profiles, its is often heavily influenced by shape similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Furr, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, when within-profile variance becomes small, variation in shape may exert a disproportionately large influence on the resulting ICCDE.
Thus, variance restrictions have a strong impact on the magnitude of the ICCDE and concomitant evaluations of construct overlaps in the sense of jingle and jangle fallacies.
Moreover, the stronger the levels of scatter of the compared profiles differ, the higher the ICCDE.
Whether such behavior is desirable depends on one's definition of profile similarity.
Last, Furr (2010) demonstrated that the magnitude of the ICCDE is largely driven by the bivariate correlation between the profiles under scrutiny.
text.formatted: Last, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Furr (2010)</ref> demonstrated that the magnitude of the ICCDE is largely driven by the bivariate correlation between the profiles under scrutiny.

text.text: Due to the mathematical interdependence, the ICCDE is sensitive to essentially the same determinants as the bivariate correlation coefficient r.

The aforementioned limitations have important implications for the fidelity of the ICCDE, as represented through the breadth of the corresponding confidence intervals, even in large samples: For instance, Blötner (2025) proposed a bootstrapping approach to estimating confidence intervals around empirically observed ICCDEs.
In a simulated dataset consisting of four normally distributed random variables (n = 1,000), an ICCDE as large as -.662 was observed for the profile similarity between two particular variables.
The 95% confidence interval around this ICCDE, however, ranged from -.999 to .398.
The extreme breadth of this confidence interval does not allow for meaningful conclusions in the context of overlaps BENCHMARK OF THE ICCDE 10 between correlation profiles.
Of note, the four variables subjected to the analyses consisted of randomly generated numbers, suggesting that all variables are uncorrelated.

Therefore, the off-diagonal elements of the correlation matrices produced across the iterations from the bootstrapping procedure can be expected to be narrowly dispersed around r = 0, which also suggests low levels of scatter in the analyzed vectors of correlations.

As a result, random variations of shape (dis)similarity occurred across the iterations, while scatter and elevation were almost constant across iterations, further suggesting that the element-wise comparisons between the correlation profiles elicited only small numerical differences.
The Open Science Framework supplement of this study entails an example with a simulated dataset comprising 20 instead of four random variables.
Therein, the same pattern holds.
The findings suggest that, particularly under low-scatter conditions, ICCDE values may be dominated by shape similarity despite also being mathematically influenced by elevation and scatter.

Since each element of a correlation profile contributes to the nomological network of a measure (Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Cronbach & Meehl, 1955), dissimilarities in the patterns of correlations observed for to-be-compared measures concerning scatter, elevation, and shape also pose indicators of differential construct validity.
text.formatted: Since each element of a correlation profile contributes to the nomological network of a measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cronbach & Meehl, 1955)</ref>, dissimilarities in the patterns of correlations observed for to-be-compared measures concerning scatter, elevation, and shape also pose indicators of differential construct validity.

text.text: Differential patterns of correlations with external variables, in turn, underscore the absence of a jangle fallacy or the existence of a jingle fallacy (Blötner, 2025; Gonzalez et al., 2021; Lawson & Robins, 2021).
text.formatted: Differential patterns of correlations with external variables, in turn, underscore the absence of a jangle fallacy or the existence of a jingle fallacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blötner, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gonzalez et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lawson & Robins, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: To reliably make such conclusions, researchers require a principled framework for evaluating overall agreement between profiles.
The present study does not seek to provide a definitive demonstration that the ICCDE is generally unsuitable as an index of profile similarity.

Rather, the goal is to specifically examine how the ICCDE behaves when applied to correlation profiles, a context in which the coefficients are bounded, mathematically constrained, and often exhibit relatively low levels of within-profile variability.

In this vein, Furr (2010) demonstrated analytically that the ICCDE reflects a combination of shape, elevation, and scatter similarity and illustrated how these characteristics affect the coefficient, but he applied these considerations to profiles of test scores that can theoretically take on all possible values between -∞ and +∞.

text.text: The present manuscript does not argue that correlation profiles require an entirely new theory of profile similarity.

Rather, the practical importance of the problem differs because correlation profiles frequently exhibit substantially lower within-profile variance than test profiles consisting of personality, ability, or clinical characteristics.
Thus, correlation profiles constitute a domain in which previously identified weaknesses of the ICCDE may be particularly likely to occur.
The present study therefore should not be viewed as a replacement for these earlier critiques, but rather as an extension of them to the specific context of nomological network comparisons.
More specifically, the contribution of the present study is threefold.
First, it investigates situations in which shape, scatter, and elevation similarities vary simultaneously rather than in isolation.

Second, it examines the behavior of the ICCDE under constraints imposed by correlation coefficients and the rule by Yule (1922) (see Equation 1) that determines the possible range of coefficients to be observed in the manipulated profile (denoted as rY, X2), given the correlation between the variables for which the correlation profiles were tested (i.e., not the correlation between the profiles; denoted as r12) and the magnitude of the coefficients in the reference profile (denoted as rY, X1).

Third, this research evaluates the sensitivity of the index under conditions of both substantial and very low levels of within-profile variability.

Thus, the emphasis of the present work is not the discovery of a previously unknown limitation, but a systematic illustration of how known limitations manifest when the object of interest is a profile of correlations.
To systematically examine the effects of (dis)similar shapes, scatters, and elevations on the direction and magnitude of the ICCDE, eight simulation conditions were created.
Each of these conditions entails a combination of equal/different shapes, equal/different scatters, and equal/different elevations.

For each condition, 10,000 iterations were carried out in which a reference profile was created by randomly drawing 30 numbers from a uniform distribution with a minimum of -.70 and a maximum of .70 (reflecting the correlation coefficients).
This range was selected because it was deemed representative of plausible correlation coefficients usually observed in construct validation studies.
Furthermore, this range warrants substantial levels of scatter within the simulated correlation profiles.
The number of elements was chosen because it was deemed realistic for an extensive construct validation study.
A number of 10,000 iterations was chosen to obtain stable estimates of the coefficient distributions across simulations that comply with the formula by Yule (1922).

text.text: The present study examined how the ICCDE behaves under different conditions by applying it to simulated pairs of correlation profiles that varied in shape, scatter, and elevation similarity.
Moreover, the role of the magnitude of the scatter within the profiles was examined.
As such, this work provides initial evidence about the interactions between shape, scatter, and elevation (dis)similarity.
Importantly, the simulations do not establish a universal criterion against which the performance of the ICCDE can be objectively judged.
Consequently, the results should not be interpreted as proving that the ICCDE is "wrong" or generally invalid.
Instead, the simulations document how the index responds under a range of theoretically meaningful conditions.

Consistent with Furr (2010), the findings indicate that changes in shape similarity are associated with pronounced changes in the ICCDE, whereas the effects of elevation and scatter similarity appear less prominent in several conditions.

text.text: If low-scatter correlation profiles are not uncommon in analyses of nomological networks, understanding how profile similarity indices behave under such conditions is of direct practical relevance rather than merely theoretical interest.

Accordingly, the principal conclusion of the present study is not that researchers should abandon the ICCDE altogether, but rather that interpretations of the coefficient should be accompanied by consideration of the underlying profile characteristics, particularly shape, scatter, and elevation.
One implication of the present findings is that no single coefficient can fully characterize all aspects of resemblance between correlation profiles.

Following the distinction made by Cronbach and Gleser (1953) between shape, scatter, and elevation, researchers may benefit from treating profile similarity as a multidimensional construct rather than reducing it to a single omnibus value (Furr, 2010).

text.text: Under such an approach, shape similarity informs the extent to which two measures exhibit comparable patterns of stronger and weaker relations with external variables.
Elevation similarity informs whether the overall magnitudes of the correlations are comparable.
Scatter similarity reflects the extent to which the strength of differentiation among correlates is comparable across measures.
The relative importance of these components depends on the substantive research question.
In some contexts, similar shape may be sufficient evidence for theoretical overlap.
In other contexts, discrepancies in elevation or scatter may be theoretically meaningful and inconsistent with claims of redundancy.
Consequently, researchers should explicitly justify which aspects of similarity are most relevant to their conclusions rather than relying exclusively on a single summary coefficient.

text.text: However, explicit theoretical criteria for determining which aspects of profile similarity are most relevant in different research contexts have not yet been articulated clearly.
Developing such criteria represents an important prerequisite for evaluating and comparing profile similarity indices in future research.
The present study provides a systematic examination of the behavior of the ICCDE when applied to correlation profiles.

Accordingly, the contribution of the present study is not the identification of a previously unknown limitation of the ICCDE, but the demonstration of how previously recognized characteristics of the coefficient may manifest in an important and commonly encountered application domain.
The findings do not suggest that the coefficient is universally invalid, nor do they overturn previous theoretical analyses.
Rather, they indicate that conclusions based on the ICCDE may depend substantially on shape similarity and on the amount of variation contained within the profiles under investigation.
Accordingly, researchers should exercise caution when interpreting the ICCDE as a standalone indicator of similarity between nomological networks.
At minimum, the coefficient should be supplemented with information about shape, scatter, and elevation, alongside graphical inspection of the profiles themselves.

text.text: Future research should focus not only on evaluating alternative omnibus indices, but also on developing principled frameworks for integrating multiple dimensions of profile similarity into substantive conclusions.

That said, the present conclusions pertain specifically to the use of ICCDE for comparing correlation profiles and should not be interpreted as a general rejection of the coefficient across all profile similarity applications.

text.text: Its eligibility as an index of the similarity between correlation profiles, however, has not yet been evaluated systematically, but only anecdotally on the basis of pre-specified profiles.

For instance, Hilbig et al. (2021) demonstrated that, despite clear element-wise differences, the ICCDE posits the vectors X1 = [.03, .01, .02] and X2 = [.51, .52, .53] as mutual opposites, ICCDE = -1.00.

In turn, Hilbig et al. showed that, despite clear element-wise correspondence between the elements of the vectors Y1 = [.29, .31, .30] and Y2 = [.30, .30, .29], the corresponding ICCDE indicates almost perfect distinctiveness, ICCDE = -.06.

These exemplary cases point to cases in which the ICCDE may indicate substantial similarity despite pronounced element-wise discrepancies (see the profiles X1 and X2) and oversees existing similarity (see vectors Y1 and Y2).
